A simple guide to making your own deep-cycle energy storage solution.

Most garages have a stack of old lead-acid batteries that are no longer fit for purpose and on their way to recycling, these can be obtained cheaply or sometimes even free if you ask nicely, they can be simply repurposed using household Alum powder and distilled water. Here's how:

  1. Drain the sulphuric acid into a suitable container (glass is best but some plastics are suitable in the short term, google it) this is quite dangerous (around 30% acid strength) so use gloves, goggles and an apron in a well ventilated safe space. The acid can be re-used as a drain cleaner but it is contaminated with lead so unless you can arrange filtering and cleaning by electrolysis it's best to take it to a suitable recycling centre.

  2. Flush the cells several times with a small amount of dilute baking soda and distilled water until the liquid comes out clean to neutralise the acid and clean the internal plates.

  3. Make a suitable amount of alkaline electrolyte (1/10 mix of household alum powder and distilled/de-ionised water) and fill the cells equally.

  4. Charge the battery at 2-5 amps rate until 12 volts is acheived, if the battery only takes 10 volts you have a shorted cell inside (unlucky), testing the battery by charging it before conversion should avoid this, if it can take up to 11 volts it's good enough. The battery will need a 'bedding-in' period to attain full strength, 3 or 4 charge/discharge cycles should be enough but discharge at 2 amp rate or less to avoid damaging it.

  5. Enjoy your inexpensive and environmentally safer battery!

Alum batteries are deep-cycle in the extreme, tests found that they can be discharged to 1 volt repeatedly without significant damage (lead-acids are generally destroyed at 9 volts) and can give near-constant current down to 5 volts on constant cycle use, they also take a charge faster and with more amps when bedded-in but only charge to around 12 volts not 13.5 like lead-acid. They can also last for years as the plates are not damaged by acid.

Disclaimer: Do this entirely at your own risk, please be careful guys! Safety first and be responsible with the waste products please.
